stimulus.title: Potassium uptake by root tissue with and without oxygen
stimulus.text: Researchers cut equal masses of young barley root tips and placed them in flasks of a solution containing 1.0 mM potassium ions (K⁺) at 25 °C. Air was bubbled through half of the flasks. Nitrogen gas was bubbled through the other half, which removes oxygen; without oxygen, the root cells make very little ATP. At each time, root samples were rinsed and the K⁺ they had taken up was measured. Values are means of 6 flasks ± 2 SE.

table.caption: K⁺ taken up by root tissue (µmol per g of root)

checks: line graph with time on the x-axis
linear scales starting at 0 that use most of the grid
both series plotted with a key
error bars of ±2 SE at each point

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: (i) Identify the independent variable in this experiment. (ii) Justify keeping the K⁺ concentration of the solution at 1.0 mM in every flask.

rubric.point: Identifies the independent variable as the gas bubbled through the flask (air or nitrogen), that is, the presence or absence of oxygen (accept: the ATP supply of the root cells, if linked to the gas).
Justifies holding K⁺ at 1.0 mM: the outside concentration (and so the gradient) affects how much K⁺ enters, so it must be the same in both treatments for any difference to be due to oxygen/ATP.
accept: a different K⁺ concentration would change uptake by itself
so the only difference between flasks is the gas

parts.sample: (i) The independent variable is the gas bubbled through the solution: air (with oxygen) or nitrogen (no oxygen). (ii) How much K⁺ enters depends on how much K⁺ is outside, so keeping it at 1.0 mM in every flask makes sure any difference in uptake comes from the gas, not from the amount of K⁺ available.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct an appropriately labeled graph that shows the mean K⁺ taken up over time for both treatments, including error bars.

rubric.point: Correct graph type (line graph or scatterplot with points joined) with time on the x-axis and K⁺ taken up on the y-axis, each axis labeled with its unit (min; µmol per g).
accept: axes labeled Time (min) and K⁺ taken up (µmol/g)

rubric.point: Appropriate linear scales on both axes, and all ten means plotted correctly.
accept: points within half a grid square

rubric.point: Error bars drawn correctly (±2 SE) on the plotted means.
accept: each bar spans mean − 2 SE to mean + 2 SE

rubric.point: The two treatments are distinguished with a key or direct labels.

parts.sample: A line graph with Time (min) on the x-axis from 0 to 120 in steps of 30, and K⁺ taken up (µmol per g of root) on the y-axis from 0 to 10 in steps of 1. The air line rises steadily from 0 to 9.0; the nitrogen line rises to about 0.9 and levels off. Each point carries a vertical error bar of ±2 SE (for example 9.0 ± 0.6 at 120 min), and a key identifies the two lines.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine whether the K⁺ taken up at 30 minutes differs between the two treatments. Use the error bars to justify your answer.

rubric.point: States that the treatments differ (likely a real or statistically significant difference) because the ±2 SE intervals do not overlap (2.1 to 2.7 and 0.4 to 0.8).
accept: error bars do not overlap, so the difference is significant

parts.sample: They differ. The air-bubbled interval runs from 2.1 to 2.7 µmol per g and the nitrogen interval from 0.4 to 0.8; the ±2 SE error bars do not overlap, so the difference is likely real.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Root tissue contains about 0.9 mL of water per gram. Calculate the K⁺ concentration inside the air-bubbled roots at 120 minutes, in mM (µmol per mL), and use it to explain what kind of transport moved the K⁺.

rubric.point: Calculates about 10 mM (9.0 ÷ 0.9) and explains that because this is about ten times the 1.0 mM outside, K⁺ moved against its gradient, so the transport was active transport using energy (ATP).
accept: 10 mM inside versus 1 mM outside, so active transport
uptake against the concentration gradient requires ATP

parts.sample: 9.0 µmol ÷ 0.9 mL = 10 µmol per mL = 10 mM. The roots hold ten times as much K⁺ as the 1.0 mM solution, so K⁺ was moved from low to high concentration, against its gradient. That can only be active transport, powered by ATP.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: At 120 minutes, nitrogen gas replaces the air in the air-bubbled flasks. Predict how the K⁺ content of those roots will change over the next hour, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts that uptake stops (the K⁺ content levels off) and may slowly fall, because without oxygen the cells make little ATP, active transport stops, and K⁺ can leak out down its gradient from about 10 mM inside to 1 mM outside.
accept: K⁺ content stops rising because active transport needs ATP
K⁺ slowly leaks out down its gradient

parts.sample: The K⁺ content will stop rising and slowly fall. Without oxygen the root cells make very little ATP, so active transport of K⁺ stops, and K⁺, now ten times more concentrated inside than outside, slowly leaks out down its gradient.
